newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.K. police in Cambodia to help find hostage.
newsitem.headline: U.K. police in Cambodia to help find hostage.

text.p: Two British police kidnap experts helped Cambodian military on Saturday in trying to confirm reports that British mine clearer Christopher Howes was heading to freedom after escaping from Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
The British Embassy in Phnom Penh said the two British police officers were somewhere "in a forward area" of Cambodia with local soldiers but had not yet been able to confirm Howes was free.

"They are in a forward area with Cambodian officials...I had contact with them one hour and 45 minutes ago. At that time there was no confirmation of a release," a British official, who did not wish to be named, said on Saturday afternoon in reference to Howes and his Cambodian interpreter Houn Hourth.
"We regard them as freed when in British hands," he said, adding that confirmation of their freedom would be released by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (Foreign Ministry) in London.

Howes and Houn Hourth were abducted by Khmer Rouge in the northwest province of Siem Reap on March 26 as they worked with Cambodian colleagues on a humanitarian mine clearing mission for the Mines Advisory Group (MAG) of Britain.

Lieutenant General Nhiek Bun Chhay told reporters on Thursday that Howes and Houn Hourth had escaped from the hardliners' Anlong Veng base in northern Cambodia earlier this month with the help of their guards and other guerrillas who wanted to defect.

The armed forces deputy chief of staff, who could not be reached on Saturday, said they had arrived at the village of Anlong Kranh, located in jungle some 185 kilometres (115 miles) north of Phnom Penh, and were expected in the capital on Friday.
But they never showed up. A senior military official in Siem Reap province told Reuters on Friday that his troops were waiting in Anlong Kranh and had not received any news of the men.
The British official would not give the location of the forward area where the two British policemen were.
But he said the British had been in regular contact with Cambodian authorities since the hostage seizure began, adding that the Cambodians "give us reports which are cause for hope."
There was speculation the delay might be linked to terms of defection by the group -- said to include a division commander and 150 men -- accompanying Howes and Houn Hourth.

The British official said they had been aware of a defection plan for some time but would not elaborate. He said they were looking at all reports from the government and trying to determine which were true.
The Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-79 rule left more than one million people dead, reneged on a 1991 peace pact and have been fighting the coalition government formed after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
The movement has been hit by massive defections in the southwest, west and northwest since August leaving the hardliners loyal to Pol Pot hanging on to territory around Anlong Veng.
"Our prime concern is his welfare and we will examine the options in light of his health," the British official said of post-release arrangements for Howes, including press access.

He urged caution in reporting, noting that the Cambodian government had blamed media reports for the failure to rescue British back-packer Mark Slater, Australian David Wilson and Jean-Michel Braquet of France from Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
The three men were executed weeks after their abduction from a train in southern Cambodia in July 1994 after negotations for their release failed and a military operation was launched.
